title: A study he owns shares in
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a general medical ward. Your consultant, Dr Fisher, asks you to help recruit patients to a clinical study of a new device for monitoring heart rhythms.

A colleague mentions that Dr Fisher owns shares in the company that makes the device. When you look at the patient information sheet, there is no mention of this.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Ask Dr Fisher whether his interest has been declared.
options.brief: A direct question may resolve your concern.
options.detailed: His interest may already have been declared and managed, but it doesn't appear on the information sheet. Asking him directly and respectfully is a fair first step.

options.text: Recruit patients as asked, as the study has been given ethics committee approval.
options.brief: Ethics approval doesn't mean every conflict has been disclosed.
options.detailed: Ethics approval is important, but if the committee wasn't told about his interest, approval doesn't address it.

options.text: Tell patients that Dr Fisher will profit from the device.
options.brief: Undermines a colleague before the facts are known.
options.detailed: Patients may need to know about conflicts, but telling them this, before you know whether it has been declared, could be unfair and damaging.

options.text: Make sure patients you approach understand that taking part is voluntary.
options.brief: Patients must not feel pressured, whatever the conflict.
options.detailed: Patients may feel obliged to agree when their own doctors ask. Making clear that saying no won't affect their care helps protect them.

options.text: Refuse to have anything to do with the study.
options.brief: May be needed later, but doesn't address the concern.
options.detailed: You aren't obliged to take part in research, but simply refusing doesn't make sure patients are protected if the conflict hasn't been managed.

options.text: Seek advice from the trust's research and development office.
options.brief: They can check whether the conflict has been properly managed.
options.detailed: The research office oversees studies in the trust and can confirm whether conflicts have been declared and whether patients should be told about them.

options.text: Recruit only patients you think would benefit from the device.
options.brief: Selection should follow the study criteria, not your judgement.
options.detailed: This seems protective, but selecting patients outside the study criteria affects the research and doesn't address the conflict.

options.text: Report Dr Fisher to the GMC.
options.brief: Premature, as the facts aren't known.
options.detailed: If an undeclared conflict was found, it might need reporting, but you first need to establish the facts locally.

explanation.issue: This tests how you respond to a possible undeclared conflict of interest in research, protecting patients without assuming wrongdoing.
explanation.keyDetails: The information sheet doesn't mention his shares. You don't know whether the interest has been declared. Patients may feel obliged to take part.
explanation.reasoning: [A] raises it directly, [D] protects patients from pressure, and [F] gets independent advice. The distractors either ignore the concern ([B], [G]), assume wrongdoing ([C], [H]), or step back without protecting patients ([E]).
explanation.competing: [B] is the tempting option, but ethics approval only covers what the committee was told.

references.title: Identifying and managing conflicts of interest
references.note: Declaring and managing financial interests, including in research.

references.title: Decision making and consent
references.note: Making sure patients' decisions to take part are voluntary and informed.
